blocks.prompt: The House You Could Not Break Into
blocks.text: A castle was not just a home. It was a home nobody could break into. The walls were stone, and some were thicker than a car is long. A deep ditch went all the way around. Some ditches held water. Some were just dry and steep. To get in, you crossed a bridge, and the guards could pull that bridge up. Then you came to the gate. Above the gate hung a heavy iron grid called a portcullis. The guards could drop it in one second. There was only one way in, and the castle could slam it shut.

blocks.prompt: A Castle Is a Machine
blocks.text: A castle looks like a building. It works like a machine, and every single part of it has a job. Start with the ditch. A wide ditch kept battering rams and rolling towers from ever reaching the wall. Sometimes it held water. Water was better, because water stopped enemies from digging underneath. Then look at the gate. The gate was the weakest spot, so builders piled defenses onto it. A bridge that lifted. A heavy iron grid, the portcullis, that dropped from above. A long dark passage with holes in the ceiling, so defenders could drop rocks on anyone who got that far. Now look at the windows. From the outside they are thin slots, barely wider than your hand. An arrow can fly out. An arrow can almost never fly in. Inside, that slot opens into a wide stone room, so the archer can step left and right and aim all along the wall. None of it was decoration. Every slot, every ditch, every corner was there because someone had tried it the other way and lost.

notes: Motte: the earth mound. Bailey: the yard

Square corners could be mined and dropped

Round towers have no corner to dig under

blocks.prompt: The Castle Kept Changing Its Mind
blocks.text: The first castles the Normans built in England were not stone at all. They were dirt and wood, and they went up fast. Workers piled a mound of earth called a motte, planted a wooden tower on top of it, and fenced a yard below called a bailey. A crew could raise one in a few weeks. That speed was the entire point. After 1066, the Normans needed to hold down a country they had only just conquered, and a hundred rough forts did that job better than one perfect one ever could. But wood burns. Within a lifetime, those mounds were carrying square stone keeps instead, with walls that arrows could not touch and fire could not eat. Then attackers found the flaw. A square tower has corners, and a corner is where stone is weakest. Miners dug a tunnel underneath it, propped the tunnel roof with timber, and then set the timber alight. When the props burned through, the tunnel collapsed, and the corner of the tower came down with it. In 1215, King John's miners brought down a corner of the great keep at Rochester in exactly that way. Builders answered by taking the corners away. A round tower has no weak edge to dig under, and stones glance off a curve instead of striking it square. Then came the best idea of all: rings. A concentric castle wrapped one wall inside another, and the inner wall was built taller, so archers standing on it could shoot clean over the heads of the archers below them. To reach the middle, you had to break through everything, twice over, while both walls shot at you the whole way.

answers: the motte is the earth mound with the tower on top; the bailey is the fenced yard below it
(inference: they had just conquered the country and needed to hold many places at once, fast)

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Most castles fell to hunger, not heroics
Wells were sunk inside the walls
Defenders countermined: tunnel against tunnel
Cannon flattened high walls from the 1400s
Star forts replaced castles: low, thick, angled
A siege cost the attacker a fortune per day

blocks.prompt: Castles Were Built to Be Boring
blocks.text: Movies show a siege as a wave of ladders and screaming. Real sieges were mostly waiting, and the castle was engineered to win at waiting. An attacker had four ways in, and three of them were bad. Storming the wall with ladders cost lives by the hundred and usually failed anyway. Battering the gate meant working directly under the murder holes, where defenders dropped rocks through the ceiling or poured water on the fires you had just lit. Mining under a corner genuinely worked, but it took weeks of digging, and defenders who heard the picks could sink a tunnel of their own and meet the miners underground in the dark. The fourth way was to sit down and wait. No food goes in, no messages come out, and eventually somebody inside opens the gate. That is how most castles actually fell: hunger, disease, or a bargain. Not heroics. So builders designed for the waiting game. They sank wells inside the walls, because a castle with its own water cannot be made thirsty. They dug cellars for grain and salted meat. A well-stocked castle could hold out for a year, and an army camped in the mud outside for a year had troubles of its own. It ran out of food too. It caught disease. It cost a fortune every single day it stood there. Time was the castle's real weapon, and the castle usually had more of it. Then, in the 1400s, gunpowder rearranged the whole argument. Cannon did not care about height. A tall thin stone wall, the pride of every castle in Europe, turned out to be the easiest target imaginable. It could not dodge, and it shattered when struck. Walls that had stood for three hundred years came down in days. The answer was to build the opposite of a castle. Engineers dropped the walls low, packed them thick with earth so that cannonballs sank in instead of smashing through, and angled them into sharp points so no attacker could stand anywhere without being shot at from the side. Seen from above, these forts look like stars. They are squat, ugly, brilliant, and they are what replaced the thing you picture when somebody says the word castle. The castle did not lose a battle. It lost an argument about physics.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Neuschwanstein, Bavaria: begun 1869
Designed first by a theater scenery painter
It has flushing toilets and central heating
The Throne Hall is built on a steel frame
It never defended anything, ever
It is the model for the castle in your head

blocks.prompt: The Castle in Your Head Is a Stage Set
blocks.text: Picture a castle. You almost certainly pictured pale stone towers, cone-shaped roofs, and small flags snapping in the wind. Hold on to that picture, because it is make-believe, and it is far younger than you think. Real castles were machines for holding land. They were squat, cold, dark, and relentlessly practical. Windows shrank to arrow slits because a window is a hole an arrow can come through. Towers went round because a square corner can be tunneled under and dropped. Ditches were dug wide because a wide ditch keeps a battering ram out of reach. Nothing on a working castle was there to look charming. Charm does not stop an army. By the 1500s, cannon had made all of it pointless. High stone walls could not dodge and could not absorb, and gunners knocked them flat. Europe stopped building castles and started building low, thick, star-shaped forts that nobody has ever put in a fairy tale. The castle should have ended right there, as a piece of obsolete military engineering. Instead it came back three centuries later as a costume. In 1869, a young king named Ludwig II of Bavaria laid the foundation stone of a castle above a gorge in the Alps. Ludwig had inherited a crown with the power drained out of it. Bavaria had backed the losing side in a war with Prussia, and within two years his kingdom would be folded into a German Empire run from Berlin. He would keep the title of king and almost none of the job. So he built himself a different century to live in. He did not begin with an architect. He began with Christian Jank, a man who painted scenery for the theater in Munich. The first drawings of Neuschwanstein were stage sets. An architect was brought in afterward, to work out how to make a painting stand up. What Jank drew was a Middle Ages that had never existed: soaring, clean, romantic, arranged for the view. The rooms inside were decorated with scenes from Richard Wagner's operas and the old legends behind them, swan knights and singing contests and doomed lovers. It was a fantasy about a fantasy. And it was thoroughly, aggressively modern. Behind the medieval face, Neuschwanstein had hot-air central heating, running water on every floor, toilets that flushed themselves, hot and cold taps in the kitchen, an electric bell system so Ludwig could summon a servant from any room, and telephone lines on the upper floors. The Throne Hall, which looks like it was hauled out of the year 1200, is built around a steel frame. The whole place is a nineteenth-century industrial building wearing armor. It never defended anything. It was never meant to. It holds no position worth the name, keeps no soldiers, and serves no purpose except to be the inside of one man's head, at enormous scale, in stone. The money ran out, because it always does. Ludwig paid with his own fortune, then with borrowed money, and the debts climbed until his ministers had had enough. In June 1886 a commission of doctors declared him insane, most of them without having examined him. He was removed from the throne. Four days later he was found dead in a lake, and nobody has ever settled how. Seven weeks after that, his government opened his private dream to paying visitors, and it has been open ever since. More than a million people walk through it every year, and a great many of them come away with their idea of what a castle is. Disney's designers came away with theirs. The pointed towers on the sheet in front of you trace back to that gorge in Bavaria, not to any fortress that ever held a wall. So the castle you imagine is not a memory of the Middle Ages. It is a stage set, built by a king with nothing left to rule, and we have all quietly agreed to believe in it.
